final_recommendation: The room converged on a trilateral USMCA package with explicit carve-outs: auto rules (75% RVC, 40% labor-value), Chapter 19, and labor enforcement locked through the 16-year review; dairy quota (3-4%) binding; trilateral labor audits symmetric. Legal drafting authorized with ratification support from Congress, Mexico, and Canada contingent on seeing final text.
key_conflicts: Initial U.S. ultimatum to proceed bilaterally without Canada triggered immediate pushback from all stakeholders
Sunset clause uncertainty threatened supply-chain investment until converted to 16-year review with explicit carve-outs
Product modernization scope ambiguity nearly derailed the deal until USTR clarified auto rules excluded from review
key_concessions: U.S. accepted trilateral (not unilateral) labor inspection committees to preserve Mexican sovereignty
Canada offered 3-4% dairy quota on cheese and milk powder
U.S. carved labor disputes out of Chapter 19, routing them through tariff enforcement instead
All parties locked auto RVC, labor floors, and Chapter 19 out of 16-year review scope
red_lines: Canada: Chapter 19 dispute settlement mechanism non-negotiable
Canada: Supply management core principle, only modest dairy access acceptable
Mexico: Trilateral (not U.S.-only) labor enforcement to preserve sovereignty
Congress/Labor/Auto: Labor-value floors and auto RVC must not reopen at review or ratification fails
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Actual legal drafting timeline and potential for language drift between verbal agreement and final text
Domestic ratification process complexity in all three countries beyond congressional committee support
Implementation and compliance costs for suppliers to meet 40% labor-value floor not quantified
Enforcement capacity of trilateral labor committees (staffing, funding, dispute resolution) not detailed
downstream_risk_variables: Legal team's ability to translate verbal commitments into airtight carve-out language within hours
Congressional committee vote timing and potential for amendments during ratification
Canadian and Mexican government ratification processes and domestic political opposition
Supplier readiness to document compliance with labor-value and RVC thresholds
Trilateral labor committee operational design and dispute resolution procedures
uncertainty_notes: Final text not yet drafted; ratification timelines in all three countries uncertain; trilateral labor audit operational details (staffing, funding, dispute procedures) unspecified; supplier compliance costs and sourcing adjustments not quantified; enforcement mechanisms for symmetric audit access not detailed.

marker_evidence.auto_rules_bottleneck: Auto RVC/labor-value carve-out from review was the final blocking issue in R4-R5; all stakeholders (Congress, auto, labor, supply-chain) demanded explicit lock-in or threatened to kill ratification
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_key: Trilateral labor committee structure with symmetric audits and tariff enforcement was the core mechanism that unlocked Canada's participation and Congress's ratification support
marker_evidence.canada_dairy_final_issue: Canada offered 3-4% quota as concession but was not the primary blocking issue; Chapter 19 and labor enforcement dominated the negotiation
marker_evidence.dispute_settlement_canada_redline: Canada stated Chapter 19 'non-negotiable' and 'not a bargaining chip'; carving labor disputes out of Chapter 19 was the compromise that preserved the mechanism and unlocked the deal
marker_evidence.sunset_to_review_compromise: Hard sunset clause threatened supply-chain investment; converting to 16-year review with explicit carve-outs was the compromise that secured business and congressional support
marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress explicitly conditioned committee support on seeing carve-out language in final text; ratification window and domestic political constraints shaped every major concession
marker_evidence.supply_chain_adjustment: Supply-chain manufacturers raised capex freeze and re-sourcing concerns but did not drive specific proposals; acknowledged as background constraint
marker_evidence.us_mexico_first_pressures_canada: Initial U.S.-Mexico bilateral was mentioned as leverage but immediately rejected by all parties; trilateral approach dominated from R1 onward

node: Node 1 - North American Trade Negotiation Room (after the 27 Aug 2018 U.S.-Mexico preliminary agreement, before the final trilateral USMCA package; information cutoff 2018-08-27)
